summary_html: Any person (not just mandated reporters) may submit a **voluntary report** to child-protection authorities. CAPTA requires states to maintain mechanisms for intake, confidentiality, and immunity policies tied to federal funding. In Alabama the age of majority is 19 (Ala. Code § 26-1-1), and for child abuse and neglect reporting a "child" is a person under 18, or a person under 19 who is in need of protective services and does not qualify for adult protective services (Ala. Code § 26-14-1(3)). Alabama is not a universal-reporter state: Ala. Code § 26-14-3 sets out who must report, and Ala. Code § 26-14-4 permits any other person to report if they have reasonable cause to suspect a child is being abused or neglected, without requiring it.
authority_html: - **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — requires states to operate intake/report systems that accept voluntary reports and protect good-faith reporters

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Alabama
key_cases.holding: The court denied mandamus and upheld a protective order that, after in camera review, limited a parent's discovery of DHR child-abuse records in a dependency case to the names and information of expected witnesses, finding no abuse of discretion.
key_cases.relevance: Non-witness informants' names were protected from disclosure to the accused parent.
key_cases.quote: while this court has the authority to require a judge to exercise proper discretion, we cannot dictate the exercise of that discretion absent a showing of abuse

key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed summary judgment for a photo shop that reported nude photographs of a child to the FBI, holding that the report rested on reasonable cause under the permissive-reporting provision of Ala. Code 26-14-4 and was therefore immune under 26-14-9, and that the reporter had no duty to include the parent's innocent explanation in the report.
key_cases.relevance: This is the leading Alabama application of Ala. Code 26-14-4, which lets any person - not only a mandated reporter - report on reasonable cause to suspect abuse or neglect.
key_cases.quote: because the report was based on "reasonable cause," the statute exempts Van's Photo from liability in making the report

key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed summary judgment on outrage and family-interference claims brought against defendants alleged to have induced others to make false child-abuse reports, holding that the pre-1998 version of Ala. Code 26-14-9 gave absolute immunity because the claimed injury related directly to the reporting of suspected child abuse.
key_cases.relevance: It is the decision that made a knowingly false third-party report unactionable under the old statute, and it is the reason the Legislature added the good-faith requirement to 26-14-9 in 1998.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that the plaintiffs' claim of intentional infliction of emotional distress relates directly to these defendants' alleged reporting of suspected child abuse.

key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed dismissal of a patient's claims against the psychologists who reported his admitted abuse of two children, holding that reasonable cause to suspect abuse both authorizes a permissive report under Ala. Code 26-14-4 and satisfies the good-faith condition on immunity in 26-14-9 as amended in 1998, and that 26-14-9 impliedly repeals the psychotherapist-patient privilege to that extent.
key_cases.relevance: Marks fixes the good-faith standard that now governs every voluntary or third-party report in Alabama: reasonable cause at the time of the report.
key_cases.quote: Under the permissive reporting provision of § 26-14-4, the existence of reasonable cause triggers the authority to make a report.
